lessons.title: um, dois, três, quatro, cinco — counting to five

You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The numbers, taken apart until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Portuguese counts almost like its sister Spanish — but with two signature Portuguese twists: heavy nasal vowels, and a number that still changes for gender where Spanish long stopped. Spanish twins are beside each.
nasal-um — um is nasal: oong said softly through the nose, no real m. (The -m is just the spelling for nasality, as in sim, bom.)
open-e — três = trehs with an open e and the circumflex marking it.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 5 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: Portuguese, from Latin, Spanish twin, English cousins. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Cinco is spelled identically to Spanish — the two closest sisters. But watch two.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: um/uma and the gendered "two" (dois/duas)

segments.text: um is also "a/an," gendered um (masc.) / uma (fem.): um café, uma cerveja. That much matches Spanish. The surprise is two: Portuguese still inflects it — dois (masc.) / duas (fem.) — a direct survival of Latin duo (masc.) / duae (fem.). So it's dois cafés but duas cervejas. Spanish levelled this to a single dos centuries ago; Portuguese kept the old split. The rest (três, quatro, cinco) don't change.

segments.text: Give 1–5 in Portuguese. (Um, dois, três, quatro, cinco.) Which number still changes for gender, and how? (Two — dois / duas, from Latin duo/duae.) What does um/uma mean besides "one"? ("A/an.") Next: 6–10, where a Portuguese sound-shift is on full display.

lessons.title: seis, sete, oito, nove, dez — and the calendar's secret
lessons.gloss: the numbers 6–10 (and the months hidden in them)

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The numbers, taken apart until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The rest of the way to ten. Like Spanish, Portuguese hides the calendar fact — setembro–dezembro are Latin for 7, 8, 9, 10 — and one number, oito, puts a signature Portuguese sound-shift on full display.
diphthong-oi — oito = OY-too, dois rhymes with it: the oi glide.
dez = dehs (open e); the final -z is a soft "sh"/"s" in Portugal, "s" in Brazil.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 5 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: Portuguese, from Latin, Spanish twin, English cousins. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.

The star is oito. Latin octō had a -ct- cluster, and Portuguese turned every Latin -ct- into -it-: octō becomes oito, noctem becomes noite ("night"), lactem becomes leite ("milk"), factum becomes feito ("done"). So oito, noite, and leite all carry the same fingerprint — once you spot the -it-, you can often guess the Latin word had a -ct-. (Spanish took a different path: octō becomes ocho, with -ct- becomes -ch-. Same cluster, two sisters, two solutions — oito vs ocho.)

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: why the months are "off by two"

segments.text: Setembro means "7th," yet sits 9th. The old Roman year began in March, so September really was the seventh; julho and agosto (July, August) were inserted later and shoved the counting months down. The Latin numbers stuck to the month names. Every dezembro, you're saying Roman "ten" — and dez also gave Portuguese dízimo, a "tithe" (a tenth), the twin of English dime.

segments.text: Give 6–10 in Portuguese. (Seis, sete, oito, nove, dez.) What Latin cluster became -it- in oito, and one more example? (-ct-; noite from noctem / leite from lactem.) Why is dezembro Latin for "ten"? (The Roman year began in March.) Next chapter builds on this toward time and days.
